items.body: Agonised Too‘s “EYE CRY” is structured around a refusal of extremes. Its artwork contains neither pure black nor pure white, and Bartosz Hervy describes the music in almost exactly the same terms: it remains close to black, occasionally approaches brightness, but always stops somewhere in the greys between them. That is more than an aesthetic decision. Across the record, vulnerability is rarely presented without some form of resistance, melody can offer access to difficult emotions while simultaneously threatening to make them too comfortable, and distance can function both as protection and as withdrawal. It also makes “EYE CRY” a marked departure from “Summer Suffering”. Hervy describes the first album as a deliberate engagement with the 1980s and New Romanticism, including the familiar contradiction between brighter music and considerably sadder lyrical content. The releases that followed were already moving elsewhere, but “EYE CRY” makes that change explicit: colder, broader in its musical vocabulary and conceived as something fluid and almost trance-like, where individual sounds matter less as isolated details than as parts of a continuous emotional movement. Melody has not disappeared; Hervy now places melody and rhythm on equal footing, while deliberately working against sweetness through rougher textures, dynamic changes and arrangements continually rebuilt around Rafał Tomaszczuk’s voice. EYE CRY by Agonised Too That relationship between intimacy and scale became particularly clear at Castle Party, where the duo brought this material onto a much larger stage without inflating its emotional language. The arrangements became rawer and more physical, low frequencies gained weight, and Bartosz Hervy’s visual work expanded into something closer to an additional instrument than an illustration behind the musicians. At the same time, the chemistry between Hervy and Tomaszczuk remains grounded in a friendship of more than twenty years rather than in rigidly assigned stage roles. I spoke with Bartosz Hervy and Rafał Tomaszczuk about the movement from “Summer Suffering” towards “EYE CRY”, why difficult emotions do not require melodrama, melody as both an invitation and a risk, creating music around a voice rather than placing a voice over finished music, the visual architecture of Agonised Too, and the quieter, more cinematic territory the project may explore next. Agonised Too interview Karo: When I reviewed “Summer Suffering”, the music placed emotional unease inside an almost luminous, immediately melodic form. “Lurking Fear” already suggested a darker psychological space, while “EYE CRY” feels colder, more severe and more willing to disturb its own beauty. Did you recognise this progression while it was happening, or did each release reveal the direction only after it had been completed? Bartosz: First of all, I would like to point out that our first album, “Summer Suffering”, was a tribute to the 1980s, New Romanticism and the bands we listened to and grew up with as kids. It had a self-contained form that was meant to be based on what had been created in music back in the ’80s. It is well known that songs from that era were often ambiguous: the music was frequently sunnier and brighter while accompanied by sad, reflective lyrics. We tried to make use of that on our first album as well. However, our first EP from 2022, the subsequent singles and the singles released after “Summer Suffering” were already outlining the path we wanted to take. This direction is more musically open, definitely darker and utilises a broader set of expressive tools. With “EYE CRY”, it was also very important to us that the album felt trance-like, fluid, told a musical story and made you feel that every single sound had its proper place. Karo: “EYE CRY” is an emotionally intense title, and in less disciplined hands it could easily lead towards melodrama. The album avoids that through restraint, detail and a certain emotional intelligence. How did you decide which feelings should be spoken directly and which needed to remain concealed inside the arrangements? Bartosz: I think it came naturally. It wasn’t like we intentionally wanted to hide anything. At least from my side, all the feelings I had while composing the music were poured out immediately. However, I don’t like overly literal forms that directly expose our vulnerability or the topic we want to talk about. I think “EYE CRY” is also a slightly playful title. On the album sleeve, it is written as “EYE” “CRY”, something that is more visual, something you can see, not just hear or feel. But already by the third track, which is the title track, the name changes to “I Cry”, which is much more direct. These feelings might seem subdued because this album is not based on extremes. On a continuous spectrum, it sits somewhere close to black, but it is still a dark grey, a graphite. Sometimes it approaches brightness, almost white, but it is always an off-white or a light grey. Rafał: For many years now, Bartosz and I have been creating, together or separately, music and content brimming with emotions. These are usually difficult emotions, which we sometimes cannot name or define, yet they are so deeply rooted within us that we feel the only way out and the only salvation is to translate them into a musical or verbal message. Perhaps it is precisely because they are genuine and organic that they protect us from falling into cheap and unnatural dramas. Furthermore, having learnt from experience, we know when not to take the next step that would risk entering the “forbidden zone”, that is, resorting to cheap tricks designed to draw listeners’ attention to our emotions in an almost primitive way. We know full well that our listeners are intelligent and won’t fall for it. 🙂 That’s why we try to stay alert and keep our finger on the pulse. Being natural and conveying genuine emotions gives us, to some extent, a guarantee that we won’t fall into our own trap. Karo: Rafał, the lyrics examine coping, withdrawal and the need to create distance from a world that can be terrifying and beautiful within the same moment. Is that distance presented as protection, or does the album also recognise the point at which self-protection becomes another form of isolation? Rafał: Keeping my distance from myself and the world in general is, alongside music, one of the most effective tools I have to protect myself. I’m no preacher; I don’t give advice on how to deal with emotions because I simply don’t know. However, by sharing what I feel, what’s inside me, I might help someone find common ground with me, and perhaps then they’ll feel a little better, perhaps they’ll understand something, feel something, or even find an answer to the issues troubling them. That’s why I find it so difficult to talk about my lyrics, and I don’t want to interpret them in my own way, as that would rob listeners of the chance to find their own meaning in them. Let everyone “play” with them according to their own rules, using their own key. Karo: The cover refuses a simple black-and-white division, and the music behaves similarly: tenderness can sit beside discomfort, while melodic clarity often carries something far less stable underneath. How important was it to leave these contradictions unresolved rather than guide the listener towards one definitive emotional interpretation? Bartosz: The album consists of shades of grey, and the cover itself, interestingly enough, is not black and white; neither pure white nor pure black was used there. It uses shades of grey that lie in between. This cover was meant to repel. If you were to compare it to feelings, at first you want to push away those heavy emotions. People who feel bad, who experience discomfort, are not always seen as welcome company. People prefer those who are smiling and cheerful, yet these problems exist within all of us. Often, people who seem smiling and very friendly on the surface are hiding something inside. We live in very anxious, overstimulated times, and many people feel this discomfort inside while not showing it on the outside. On the cover, we showed a greater level of discomfort than what you actually experience while listening to the album. For me, as the creator of the graphic design and the band’s visual materials, this was a complete counterweight to the cover of “Summer Suffering”, which was almost glamour: yellow with a black, disco-ball-style heart. Here, we wanted to go in a completely different direction. The cover looks as if someone has already damaged it. People say it looks worn out, but it’s simply a graphic meant to signify that there are scratches somewhere inside and we need to pay attention to them. Karo: Melody remains fundamental to Agonised Too, even as the production on “EYE CRY” becomes colder and more experimental. How do you recognise the point at which melody gives the listener necessary access to a difficult emotion, and the point at which it might make that emotion too attractive or too easy to consume? Bartosz: I know that Rafał is a huge fan of melody. I am too. The older I get, the more I believe that melody is the foundation of music, alongside rhythm. There was a time when rhythm was more important to me, but now melody and rhythm stand on equal footing. I try to balance it so as not to make the album too “sugary”, which I personally couldn’t identify with, because I always prefer rougher content and blending contrasts. Dynamic, almost cinematic changes have always been crucial to me. I tried to make sure everything had its place: the vocals and lyrics had to be clear, sometimes enhanced with audio effects. There is a lot of melody in the vocals, so you have to tread lightly to avoid oversweetening it. On the other hand, the rhythm is meant to be trance-like. I like trance, I like how songs flow and change while still forming an integral whole. Rafał: What Bartosz says is very important. Generally speaking, we’re all looking in the same direction, but each of us sees things through a different lens. Perhaps that is precisely where the key to our “success” lies. Karo: Bartosz, the album contains considerable sonic detail, yet it rarely feels crowded. There is pressure, but also carefully protected space around Rafał’s voice. How do you construct that balance? Do you begin by building the electronic environment, or by identifying the emotional space the vocal needs in order to remain exposed? Bartosz: We create in a rather interesting way. Rafał gets initial outlines of the tracks to familiarise himself with them, then he writes the lyrics and sings. At the same time, I keep working on the backing track, so a second or third version of the music is often created before the demo vocals are even recorded. However, once the actual vocals arrive, I write and rebuild the music directly around them so that everything forms a unity. The point is for the vocals not to feel like an element just glued onto a finished backing track, but for the whole thing to sound like a single, organic organism. Karo: Your Castle Party performance was splendid because the intimacy of “EYE CRY” survived the scale of the Castle Stage. The low frequencies became more physical, Rafał’s delivery carried much farther, and the material seemed larger without becoming emotionally inflated. What did you change in the arrangements or performance to make these songs inhabit such a large open space? Bartosz: I always try to prepare the arrangement slightly differently for live performances compared to the album. An album follows its own rules: frequencies must be balanced so that it is pleasant to listen to repeatedly without fatigue. Live, aside from the fact that we play part of the material live and the vocals are live, I like to boost the low frequencies and bring out elements that are subtler on the album. I like to push certain instruments to the front and hide others. I simplify the arrangement a bit, but I make it rawer and more emotional, so that it overwhelms the listener in a very positive sense, making them feel the music not just with their ears, but with their entire body. Rafał: Thank you for your kind words about our performance. 🙂 As Bartosz says, each of our gigs is slightly different. I won’t hide the fact that before the Castle Party gig I had some concerns, which I mentioned to Bartosz. They were about the size of the stage and whether we’d feel “isolated” on it as a duo. It’s hard for just the two of us to fill that space in a way that holds the audience’s attention. Fortunately, my concerns turned out to be unfounded because, thanks to Bartek’s brilliant visuals and the chemistry we share during our performances, we were able to fill that space on our own terms. Karo: Bartosz, the Castle Party visualisations were among the most precisely integrated I saw during the festival. They did not illustrate the lyrics literally; at times they followed the music, while elsewhere they seemed to resist it through delay, distortion or disappearance. Did you design them as a parallel narrative, an emotional counterpoint, or as another instrument within the performance? Bartosz: Visualisations are another instrument in our performance and an integral part of who we are. We always play with them. Since I do this professionally, creating and editing video, it was natural to incorporate this element into Agonised Too. I always say that I simply think in images. When I listen to music or when Rafał and I discuss a new track, I see images in my head first, and only then comes the sound. So, the visualisations are another layer of the show for us. Some of them are reworked music videos, while others were created exclusively for the live set. I want the audience to get that “third factor”. At Castle Party, we had incredible opportunities. Seeing these videos on such a massive screen amplified the emotions. Watching the concert footage afterwards, I thought to myself: “Cool, that’s exactly what I wanted, that’s how it was supposed to look.” Karo: Onstage, Rafał appears to carry the vulnerable human centre of the material, while Bartosz controls the electronic and visual architecture surrounding him. How carefully is that relationship constructed, and how much freedom remains for one of you to alter the emotional direction of a song during the performance? Bartosz: This relationship stems from the fact that Rafał and I have known each other for over 20 years and we are friends. We talk practically every day. The distance, the fact that I live between Gdańsk and Poznań, and Rafał lives in Białystok, has absolutely no impact on the emotions in our music. Onstage, we want to be integrated, but each of us retains our own personality. Nothing is artificially staged or forced; we don’t have rigid expectations of each other. In electronic music, where there are only two people on stage, authenticity is paramount. We simply rely on natural energy, and that complements us well. Rafał: You’ve put it perfectly. Bartosz and I work instinctively, fitting the pieces of the whole together seamlessly. It’s a sort of instinct that allows us to tune our radars to the same frequency. This gives us a freedom that, in turn, translates into the studio and live quality of our music. Of course, our long-standing friendship, which Bartosz mentioned, helps us a great deal in this! Karo: After “Summer Suffering”, “Lurking Fear”, “EYE CRY” and the experience of bringing this material to Castle Party, which part of the Agonised Too language now feels fully explored, and which element still seems unfinished, something you have discovered but have not yet pushed far enough? Bartosz: In the future, I would like us to dive even deeper into highly emotional and atmospheric tracks. Electronic music doesn’t always have to rely on a fast, danceable rhythm; there is immense power in spirituality and apparent delicacy. An example of this direction is “Fire Has Seen It All”. It is probably our least “concert-ready” track. We haven’t played it live yet, but to me, it is the most cinematic, visual and emotionally raw piece we have ever recorded. Further exploring this cinematic, deep side of Agonised Too is definitely something I want to develop on future releases. Rafał: For my part, I’ve been feeling comfortable and at ease lately with dance- and beat-driven music, which are, of course, united by a good melody, so I think our current artistic directions and visions will lead us to something unique, fresh and, most importantly, sincere in its message. About Agonised Too Agonised Too are a Polish electronic duo consisting of Bartosz Hervy and Rafał Tomaszczuk. Hervy is responsible for the project’s music, production and visual identity, while Tomaszczuk writes the lyrics and provides vocals. Their collaboration also rests on a friendship extending for more than twenty years, despite the musicians currently living in different parts of Poland. The project’s first material appeared in 2022 with the “First Track” EP on 21 December, followed by the “Type Zero” EP on 21 March 2023, both mixed and produced by Hervy at ROOM XII. The duo came out of Agonised By Love. Their first full-length album, “Summer Suffering”, released on 20 June 2024, established an aesthetic deliberately informed by the 1980s and New Romanticism, and closed on a cover of Army of Lovers’ “Obsession”. Hervy describes that record as a self-contained tribute to music the musicians had grown up with, including the characteristic contradiction between bright, melodic arrangements and reflective or melancholic lyrics. Subsequent material gradually moved towards a broader and considerably darker electronic vocabulary, through the single “The Same” on 6 August 2025 and “Safer/Stronger” on 6 June 2026. Their second album, “EYE CRY”, released on 26 June 2026, develops that change much further. Rather than relying on constant extremes, the record was conceived around gradations and contrasts: darker production, trance-like rhythmic movement, melody balanced against rougher textures and carefully protected space around Tomaszczuk’s voice. Its seven tracks are “Negative Space”, “Lurking Fear”, “I Cry”, “Fire Has Seen It All”, “Are You Afraid Of Tomorrow?”, “Safer/Stronger” and “The Same”. Hervy also created the album’s graphic identity, deliberately rejecting pure black and white in favour of damaged surfaces and shades of grey. Visual work is integral to Agonised Too rather than an accompaniment added to the music later. Hervy works professionally with video and describes himself as thinking in images, with some concert visualisations derived from music videos and others created specifically for performances. The duo treat this imagery as a “third factor” alongside sound and performance. Their Castle Party appearance on 19 July 2026, on the Castle Stage at Bolków Castle, demonstrated how that audiovisual approach can expand to a major outdoor stage. Hervy altered the arrangements by emphasising low frequencies, simplifying certain components and bringing previously subtle elements forward, while Tomaszczuk’s initial concern about whether two performers could occupy such a large stage was ultimately answered by the combination of their chemistry and the scale of the visual production. The next direction may emerge from an interesting tension already visible between the two musicians. Hervy wants to push further into cinematic, atmospheric and emotionally exposed material, naming “Fire Has Seen It All” as the deepest example of that side of Agonised Too so far, while Tomaszczuk currently feels especially drawn towards dance- and beat-driven music anchored by strong melody. Rather than pointing towards two contradictory futures, those instincts may simply extend the method already at work on “EYE CRY”: allowing different emotional and musical states to coexist without forcing them into a single colour.

items.body: Nine years after “The Gag File”, Aaron Dilloway has a new solo album. The American experimental musician releases “No Skill Comedy Mind Reading” on Dais Records on 30 October 2026, his third proper solo LP and the first since 2017. Dilloway builds the record from 8-track tape loops, feedback-shrouded found sounds, field recordings and vocal improvisation, and it collects material drawn from close to a decade of solo work. No Skill Comedy Mind Reading by Aaron Dilloway Dilloway treats the album as the closing part of a set of three. He described the connection between them in the announcement, and he did so without separating the humour from the damage: “I almost feel like they’re kind of part of one piece. All three records are trying to find humor in the worst possible situations. Depending on who is listening and what their mindset is, they could be seen as funny or just horrifying, horrible records.” The sequence starts with “Modern Jester”, issued by his own Hanson Records in 2012, and runs through “The Gag File”, his first release for Dais Records in 2017. Eight tracks make up the album: “Raw Hyde”, “My Brain Has Finished Growing”, “Forced Auctioneer”, “Find A New Way To Laugh”, “Bring Me The Head Of The Unknown Comic”, “Possession Audition Tape”, “The Levitation Hacker” and “Supporting Actor (for Pieter & Phil)”. Dais Records has shared the first track, “Find A New Way To Laugh”, as official audio, and the album is available to pre-order. What shaped ‘No Skill Comedy Mind Reading’ Three reference points sit behind the record: the sound design of Alvin Lucier, Andy Milligan’s low-budget 1989 horror film “The Weirdo”, and the film composer Hugo Montenegro. Dilloway acquired a set of Montenegro’s belongings through a storage-unit auction, including notes from the composer’s early electronic experiments, and material from that find feeds several of the album’s more unsettled passages. The laughter running through “Bring Me The Head Of The Unknown Comic” nods sonically to Nurse With Wound and thematically to the paper-bag-headed 1970s American television comedian. Tape hiss is treated as material rather than as a defect. Dilloway traces that back to the cassettes he was given as a teenager, by the Misfits and Circle Jerks among others, on which the artifacts of repeated dubbing had become part of what he was hearing: “I am into the idea of building all of these layers and turning them into something else. Like when I play live, things can get harsher than my recorded music, and for this, I wanted to get that feeling, for these blasts to be loud, but a bit more subdued. That complete static sound, almost like you’re underwater.” The drone that opens the album comes from two Nepali sarangi bows rubbed against each other, an instrument Dilloway encountered during the period he spent living and recording in Nepal from late 2004. On the B-side, “Possession Audition Tape” cuts up phrases he reads from a book about an eighteenth-century French religious group given to public disruption. The closing “Supporting Actor (for Pieter & Phil)” is a synth and organ rhythm-machine piece derived from music he made for Pieter Schoolwerth and Phil Vanderhyden’s film “Supporting Actor”. The album took shape alongside other work. “This record has kind of consumed my head since I finished ‘The Gag File’ [2017]. At first, I was thinking it would be more of a pop record, but then the Lucrecia project kind of got that out of my system. It started to flow more like my live sets,” Dilloway said, referring to “Lucy & Aaron”, his 2021 album with Lucrecia Dalt. Aaron Dilloway tour dates 2026 Dilloway plays five US shows across September and October: 25 September 2026 – Los Angeles, CA, USA – Threshold 26 September 2026 – Cleveland, OH, USA – The Bent Mace 8 October 2026 – Chicago, IL, USA – Empty Bottle 9 October 2026 – Louisville, KY, USA – The B-Side 30 October 2026 – Pittsburgh, PA, USA – Woodstreet Galleries About Aaron Dilloway Aaron Dilloway was born on 13 May 1976 and grew up in Brighton, Michigan. As a teenager he began going to house shows in nearby Ann Arbor, formed the group Galen in the 1990s and then joined Couch, the band Galen had opened for at its first show. After moving to Ann Arbor he played with experimental and noise groups including Universal Indians, and co-founded Wolf Eyes, with which he performed until 2004. Late in 2004 he moved to Nepal, where he recorded his own material, field recordings and Nepalese radio broadcasts. He relocated to Ohio in 2007, worked with Emeralds among others, and settled in Oberlin, where he runs the label, record shop and mailorder Hanson Records. His first solo LP, “Modern Jester”, appeared on Hanson Records in 2012, and “The Gag File” followed on Dais Records in 2017. Between the two he kept up a steadier flow of tape releases and collaborative records. Two collaborative albums arrived in 2021: “Lucy & Aaron” with Lucrecia Dalt on Hanson Records, and “Body/Dilloway/Head” with Kim Gordon and Bill Nace’s Body/Head on Three Lobed Recordings. He has also realised John Cage’s 88-tape-loop piece “Rozart Mix” and written an original score for “The Absence of Milk In The Mouths of the Lost”. “No Skill Comedy Mind Reading” is his third solo album and his second for Dais Records, arriving nine years after the last one.

items.body: Joy Division’s Shadowplay has been covered enough times to qualify as communal property, which means anybody taking another swing at it ought to bring a crowbar. Fear Maintenance does. The solo project of Burlington, Ontario, musician Colin Adams takes one of the bleak monuments of post-punk and drags it through heavier machinery, replacing some of the original recording’s metallic distance with guitars that hit closer to Ministry and an industrial-metal undertow that makes the song feel physically larger. Somewhere inside it, a factory alarm discovers religion beneath a collapsing cathedral roof, and the song looks newly dangerous. Adams created Fear Maintenance to “simultaneously pay homage to and reimagine some of the darker iconic songs from the post-punk bands of the late 1970s and 1980s, which inspired him to become a musician.” That intention could have produced reverent cosplay, the sort of embalmed tribute that treats 1979 as sacred territory. Instead, Adams seems more interested in the violence already latent in the song. Joy Division could sound brutally alive onstage, with the rhythm section pushing forward while guitars scraped against the walls, and Adams uses that live ferocity as his point of departure. Played, produced, and recorded entirely in his Burlington home studio, this Shadowplay incarnation thickens the low end and lets the guitars bear more weight. The familiar architecture remains recognizable, yet its surfaces have been roughed up, with industrial pressure gathering around the vocal and percussion. The result sits in a strange corridor between goth, post-punk, and metal, where Ian Curtis’s fatalism suddenly has steel-toed boots. Watch the video below: Homage becomes interesting when somebody risks damaging the shrine. Adams keeps the song’s bones while giving its muscles a different chemistry, and his heavier approach finds aggression inside material often remembered chiefly for austerity. Shadowplay survives the treatment because it was always tougher, stranger, and more dangerous than the museum glass surrounding Joy Division might suggest. items._cn_summary: Fear Maintenance是加拿大安大略省Burlington音乐人Colin Adams的独立项目，他对Joy Division经典曲目《Shadowplay》进行了重新解构。这首翻唱全程在家中工作室录制完成，将原曲冰冷的金属质感替换为更厚重的吉他音墙，借鉴Ministry式的工业金属音色与工业金属的暗流，让歌曲在体量上物理性地膨胀。低频被刻意加厚，吉他承担了更多重量，熟悉的架构仍可辨认，但表面被工业压力打磨得粗粝。整体落在goth、post-punk与metal之间的奇特走廊，Ian Curtis的宿命感被装上了钢头靴。项目初衷是向七十年代末八十年代初的后朋克经典致敬，但Adams更倾向于挖掘歌曲中潜在的暴力美学与现场演出的原始烈性，而非制作一具博物馆式的纪念标本。

items._cn_summary: Tempalay的《ATOMEW》以"新原子"为概念起点，描绘从虚无中诞生新生命与新世界的过程。专辑结构具有清晰叙事弧线：开篇以渐进摇滚的宏大尺度奠定基调，中段穿插变拍子驱动的噪音嘻哈与电子声响，尾声以乐队自成一格的福音曲式收束。整体制作围绕极简律动骨架展开，在精细编配与大胆音色之间寻找平衡，营造出类似科幻电影的沉浸感。乐队延续此前对后摇滚语汇的拓展，但本次在声音设计上更为激进，将不同时代与类型的美学并置于同一框架内，形成具有异世界质感的听觉空间。

items.body: Review by yarstruly — Simultaneously posted to my blog (Scott's Song by Song Spotlights) with links for listening and purchasing.Today's album is slightly older than my more recent reviews, but certainly not an old album. Released on December 5 of 2025, "Elliptical Passage" is a collaboration between Barry Cleveland and Robert Rich (no relation to me that I am aware of). According to the press release I have received:Barry Cleveland is an LA-basedcomposer, guitarist, recordist,journalist, and author. His sevenalbums showcase a range of stylesfrom ambient to avant-rock to worldfusion. Cleveland also penned thecult classic book Joe Meek's BoldTechniques, and served as an editorat Guitar Player magazine for 12years. (barrycleveland.com)Robert Rich has released over 60albums across five decades,defining his unique language ofambient electronic music. Richbegan building synthesizers in1976, when he was 13, and laterstudied computer music atStanford's CCRMA whileresearching lucid dreaming. His allnightSleep Concerts have becomelegendary. (robertrich.com)Barry says the album began when he discovered some decade old recordings he had made. While improvised, he felt that the ideas had musical merit, and he contacted Robert Rich about using the recordings as a basis for an album, and he agreed. Recently, Barry reached out to me about reviewing this album, and I agreed. As always, I receive no additional compensation, and I call it like I hear it. As per my usual method, this is a cold listen.Album credits:Produced by Barry Cleveland and Robert Rich.Mixed and mastered by Robert Rich.BC: Guitar, pizzicato arpeggione, bass, gongs, bowed cymbals, loopers.RR: Piano, flute, lap steel, percussion, Prophet X, Haken Continuum.All compositions by Barry Cleveland and Robert Rich.Primary guitar figure in "Zero of the Sanctified" derived from a line by Steve Rapetti. Track 1: Tangible Silence (6:55)This fades in with sustained synth chords, and swelling guitar notes. As it progresses, there are some interesting low pitched tones. The music gradually crescendos. There are no noticeable underlying rhythms. This might make a good meditation track. Various tones come in and out of the soundscape. At around 4:20 a flute takes the spotlight and most of the other sounds drop out. Different sounds gradually come back in. This reminds me of the introduction from Led Zeppelin's "In the Light". While this type of track is not in my usual wheelhouse, I can tell you that I enjoyed it and I found it to be well-done.Track 2 - Beckoning Voices (6:26)This one came so smoothly out of the first track, that I initially didn't realize that the track had changed. Once again there are long sustained sounds at first. However, a bass pattern begins to emerge, giving a sense of rhythm and momentum that the first track did not have. The overall sound, however, is still based on long, floating sustained tones. The music on this album, so far, would work as the soundtrack for a movie about space travel. The sounds are quite interesting and engaging. Later in the track, the bass pattern has dropped out, but the melodies are becoming more pronounced, with some subtle rhythms on piano. Intriguing track.Track 3 - Elliptical Passage (8:31)Once again, the transition from one track to another is seamless. A sound that makes me think of a spaceship enters the soundscape. This one feels more ominous than the first two. That said, there are some lighter tones in with the more foreboding ones. At around 3 minutes in, there are reverse recorded guitar sounds. Some harmonics are played in octave unison with a descending bass line after 4 minutes in. At around 6:45 there is a sustained guitar melody that actually reminds me of a melodi in Fleetwood Mac's everywhere. Another point of reference is that some of the sounds just before the eight minute point remind me of ones in Phil Collins' classic "In the Air Tonight". Track 4 - Gathering Stars (12:53)Once again, the transition is seamless. The guitar harmonics float on top of the sustained tones. The slide guitar notes are a recurring feature of the music. Some of the tones remind me of "In the Light" once again. I feel like we are about to "arrive" somewhere at about 8:30. This is becoming more intense as it goes along. The bass notes provide some tension and release. This is less melodic than its predecessor. The last portion has some hopeful sounding brighter tones. Track 5 - Luminous Expanse (10:51)As has been the case throughout, another seamless transition. The title implies sunrise over a wide, open area, And that is what the music implies to me as well as this track emerges. There is a subtle underlying rhythmic pattern on this one. The flute brings an organic touch to the soundscape. At around 6:40, there are some distorted power chords in the mix, but they are not the most prominent part. The guitar chords become more prominent at around 9:30. Track 6 - Zero of the Sanctified (9:30)As this one transitions out of the previous one, there are some clean guitar chords and a bit of smooth lead guitar phrases, but all still very sustained. The guitar is much stronger and more up front than it has been on the other parts of the album. This one is more horror movie soundtrack like than floating through space. The longer it goes on, the more disturbing it gets. The music calms down at around 5:30 and becomes more peaceful. The music begins to fade a bit with about one minute left, then some chime-ey guitar notes close the album out. OVERALL IMPRESSIONS:While electronic, ambient music is not really my favorite subgenre of prog, I can tell that Barry Cleveland and Robert Rich took great care in where every note and sound was placed on the album. The soundscapes are warm and rich. Fans of this genre will love this album. So, while it is not really an album that I will likely return to very often, I must reward the quality of it. I give it a 4 out of 5 stars. Or 80%. Many will rank it higher.
items._cn_summary: 这张专辑是吉他演奏家Barry Cleveland与电子音乐人Robert Rich的合作项目，基于Cleveland十年前的即兴录音素材进行再创作。Rich负责混音、合成器与多种器乐演奏，Cleveland则贡献吉他、拨弦低音、钹弓奏、循环采样等层次。整体呈现长延时持续音为主导的氛围化电子声响结构，缺乏明显节拍，部分曲目如《Tangible Silence》更接近冥想音乐特质。首两首曲目之间几乎无缝过渡，低频贝斯线条缓慢浮现提供推进感。评论者将其归入前卫电子类别，与Led Zeppelin《In the Light》引子的氛围感进行类比，表明作品带有上世纪七十年代摇滚的氛围化延伸痕迹而非纯粹实验抽象。整体属于氛围与前卫电子交汇地带，融合即兴素材与精细录音工艺。

items.body: Review by Fercandio46 — What I find interesting when listening to Mountains is, first, the use of folklore from regions bordering the band's native Finland, as if the depths of Nepal and the Himalayas were leading the way there, and second, how that same folklore lent itself, much like Middle Eastern traditions, to the sinuous, serpentine melodies characteristic of psychedelia; it is as if something ancient from the East were meeting the West to erupt into that invisible form of music. In this way, Hadal Sherpa immerses itself, with a synthesizer backdrop evoking outer space, in populating the soundscape with constellations, featuring guitar solos weaving between rhythm and lead parts, alongside a flute that highlights the desert-like, austere, and climatically violent and aggressive nature of their music. Goat Gaze will amplify these qualities with the captivating spell of a flute that dances over the psychedelic textures like a serpent.Starting with Dark Tides, one can find certain similarities to Hawkwind, yet Eastern time signatures are a constant presence, capitalizing on the sense of confusi�n, a kind of claustrophobia, arising from the relentless repetition of notes that shrink a space which, mere moments earlier, had seemed infinite.Upon listening to Ormus, one might even draw a parallel to John Zorn's Electric Masada, a comparison anchored here by the virtuosity of guitarist Vesa Pasanen. "Return to Farum Azul" breaks a certain stylistic monotony through the inclusion of a choir, lending the track an epic, palatial atmosphere."Mountains" and "Gurbet" resume the cosmic journey, drawing parallels with deserts and mountains, and that ascent into the infinite which serves as the album's central metaphor, with profound stylistic richness, though perhaps with an overly narrow focus on just one facet of that spectrum of possibilities.
items._genre: psychedelic rock / space rock / world fusion
items._cn_summary: 这是一张以东方民间音乐元素为核心、融合迷幻与太空摇滚概念的跨界作品。Hadal Sherpa来自芬兰，却以尼泊尔与喜马拉雅地区的民俗素材为切入点，将中东传统的蜿蜒旋律线条嫁接至迷幻摇滚的框架之中，形成古今东西交汇的听觉意象。专辑以合成器铺陈宇宙感的背景音色，吉他独奏在节奏与主旋律之间穿梭，笛声游走于迷幻织体之上，营造出荒漠般严酷而辽阔的氛围。部分曲目引入合唱与东方节拍，打破单一风格重复，同时与Hawkwind及John Zorn的Electric Masada形成参照。整体在迷幻摇滚范畴内具有文化视角的新颖性，但在风格光谱的开掘上稍显集中，深度有余而广度略欠。

items.body: Tuğçe Şenoğul Atlas self-released There’s precious little information in English about Turkish vocalist Tuğçe Şenoğul. Aside from references to her time as one half of Seni Görmem İmkansız, and a few scattered write-ups about various collabs, it’s hard to find much reliable on the Istanbul-based artist. With that said, her streams on Spotify and Turkish language coverage certainly attest to some degree of popularity in her home country, with her new album Atlas (following from EP of the same name a few years back) demonstrating an intriguing mixture of modern electropop and traditional folk music. How that works in practice is fairly straightforward; on tracks like “Serseri” and “Cennet” Şenoğul mixes smoky, trip-hoppy production with strings, percussion and horns, all blended with a remarkable smoothness that speaks to the overall earthy and organic vibe of the compositions. Not every track relies on the mixture of traditional and electronic instruments – the lovely opener “Kırık Hikaye” is entirely made up of electronic ambiences, while “Bu Gece” is largely a simple piano based composition – their deployment a testament to the more measured and sensuous vibe of the instrumentals. It’s of course easy for the non-Turkish listener to get caught up in the novelty of hearing these sounds and musical approaches brought together, but there’s actually an interesting tension in how complex the arrangements and songwriting performance are, and Şenoğul’s presence as a vocalist. The record is very much at its best when the instrumentation gets out of her way and lets her take all the focus. The title track features a lovely mixture of percussion and some very interesting stringed instruments along with its throbbing electronic pulse, but it’s all about hearing how she slides between each different element, forceful without needing to belt it out or even change the urgency of her delivery. The tracks with a slightly more traditional structure end up being a mixed bag; “Sensin Bunlara Sebep” is a more traditional pop take on Turkish folk but is far less intriguing than the loungey, Collide-esque sounds of “Hatıramızla”, delivered with a reserved but coy wink. While you’ve got a few tracks in the mix like “Aşk Deli” that could fit on a darkwave dancefloor alongside Kite, the real appeal of Atlas lies in its warm, enveloping production and the power of Tuğçe Şenoğul as a performer. Even without knowing a lick about the themes and topics of these songs, she cleanly communicates love, sorrow, loss and resolve, picking her spots to hold back, where she employs her full range, and knowing how each bit of phrasing and inflection effects the whole. Buy it. Atlas by Tuğçe Şenoğul The post Tuğçe Şenoğul, “Atlas” appeared first on I Die: You Die.
items._cn_summary: 土耳其歌手Tuğçe Şenoğul的专辑《Atlas》将现代电子流行与土耳其传统民间音乐融合，以烟雾感的trip-hop式制作串联弦乐、打击乐与铜管。编曲层次复杂，人声在器乐退让时获得充分展现空间，标题曲中她在不同音色间游走，无需高声呼喊即传递力度。电子氛围与简约钢琴交织，少数曲目带有暗潮舞曲的冷调气质。整张专辑以温暖包裹感的制作与歌手的演绎为核心，传达爱、悲、失落与决意。

items.body: August 14 - 16, 2026, Peitz, Germany Up a creaky set of wooden stairs to the lofts of the 1810 Huettenwerk of the historic Ironworks and Fishery Museum of Peitz, an imposing building full of old heavy tools for the iron foundry and fishing works in the surrounding carp ponds, is an exhibition on Free Jazz in the German Democratic Republic (former East Germany). It’s a traveling show, having accompanied Jazzwerkstatt concerts and festivals over the years. The first time I encountered it, at a Globe Unity Orchestra concert in Potsdam in 2014, it prompted me to dig for all of the Amiga Jazz records that I could find, leading to likely the most complete collection of East German jazz in New Jersey. Every year for the past ten years or so that I’ve been to the festival, I find myself drawn to the exhibition, like a pilgrim to worship. Each station of the exhibit offers a glimpse into this well documented but still mythical past, with a final station showcasing the Peitz Festival. Created in 1973 by two young free-thinking music fans, Uli Blobel and Peter “Jimi” Metag, both from the small East German town of Peitz, the festival drew other like minded youth to hear both East German musicians like Ernst-Ludwig Petrowsky and Conny Bauer as well as West German musicians like Alexander von Schlippenbach and other musicians from the other side of the Iron Curtain such as Barry Guy and Wadada Leo Smith. The names are many and the history can be read in the “Woodstock am Karpfenteich’ books as well as experienced here , and the story is a good one. Lasting until shut down by the government in 1982 and restarted by Blobel in 2011 under much different conditions, the Jazzwerkstatt Peitz festival of 2026 still draws some of those who trekked by train and Trabi to the original, but is also working to draw in a new audience whose connection to the past is being built by heading to upper floors via creaky wooden stairs. Starting in 2024, Marie Blobel, the daughter of Uli Blobel, took over. Some of the changes Marie Blobel made included moving the festival from the center of Peitz to the grounds of the fishing museum amidst the carp ponds and injecting a festive flair into the weekend long event. With a packed schedule of concerts and a two kilometer hike to the Doener restaurant, festival goers are oriented to the wurst stand, the home cooked vegetarian dishes at the beer tent and the biergarten around the corner. Kids have the chance to make their own music with an imaginative looping station and everyone can climb aboard the “Karpfenbummler,” an electric miniature train that will take you in style from the festival to town to the train station. Coming into its own it the new form, Jazzwerkstatt Peitz was awarded the Deutsche Jazzpreis this past year. -- Gebhard Ullman’s Hemisphere 4 PLUS (biergarten stage) The concerts began on Friday evening with the folk-meets-modern-jazz sounds of Trio Ivoire . In the trio's music, Hans Lüdemann ’s piano and electronics and Christian Thomé 's percussion and electronics are met with the organic tones of Aly Keïta ’s balafon, an African instrument described as a “ a gourd-resonated xylophone .” The music is upbeat and highly syncopated and thus quickly had some of the at-capacity audience on their feet swaying to their rhythms. As soon as the set ended, the audience began shuffling off, around the museum and cycler hostel (the Gurkenradweg - yes, the Pickle Bikepath - passes by the festival grounds), to a biergarten, where a stage has been set up under a lush copse of trees. Woodwindist Gebhard Ullman ’s newest formation, Hemisphere 4 PLUS , featuring a mix of his current electric and acoustic groups, began with a chamber-jazz like combination of Anna Viechtl ’s harp and Taiko Saito’s vibraphone. Disrupted by a crash of percussion, the group tumbled into a pulsating groove. Describing the music as “sculptures,” Ullmann led the group through an alluring mix of the delicate (add Silke Lange accordion to the chamber jazz components), hard-hitting (with Eric Schaefer on drums and Oliver Potratz on bass) and other-worldly ( Liz Kosack ’s keyboard and synthesizer). OM (main stage) A short shuffle back to the main stage where OM , the legendary avant-jazz-rock group, were ready to go. The original group members, saxophonist Urs Leimgruber , guitarist Christy Doran and bassist Bobby Burri were joined by drummer’s Gerry Hemingway and Tony Buck who have replaced the late Fredy Studer, as they did on the recent Intakt release Suedpol . After a short freely improvised intro from Leimgruber, a blast of rock energy from Doran gave root to a swirling squall of tones and the music slowly evolved into a groove led by the two percussionists. Moments of electric Miles colored the rich panoply of sound which ranged from deeply experimental to outright rock. An excellent set. Closing out the main stage for the evening was the quartet Selvhenter from Copenhagen. Saxophonist Sonja LaBianca and trombonist Maria Bertel and drummers Anja Jacobsen and Jaleh Negari crafted a dark, throbbing techno-jazz designed to get festival goers on their feet. It was quite late by the time the quartet’s final notes faded, but the show wasn’t over … yet, as drummer Willi Kellers and organizer Wolfgang ‘Assi’ Gloede were hosting a jam session in the cozy workshop building behind the main stage. Amongst painted fish sculptures and some serious looking tools, saxophonist Lotte Anker , keyboardist Liz Kosack and bassist Reza Askari joined Kellers in free-jazz improvisation that began with electronic percolations and slowly crescendoing notes that eventually balled into an exciting and thorny tumbleweed of sound. Following the opener, Gloede curated combinations of professional and hobbyist musicians who improvised into the wee hours. -- Wanja Slavin (sitting far right) (church) Saturday’s full schedule began in the town church where saxophonist and festival Improviser-in-Residence Wanja Slavin , last year’s winner of the Brandenburg Jazzpreis - an award developed by Jazzwerkstatt and the state of Brandenburg - debuted a new composition with a band comprised of Peter Evans on trumpet, Leonard Huhn on bass clarinet, Almut Kühne with vocals and Kaja Draksler on piano. The rich 45-minute piece moved seamlessly between moods and approaches as darker moments were balanced by more hopeful passages. Repetitive arpeggios and prominent electronics formed a consistent tonal base accentuated by the dissonant church organ and several outstanding solos. A short while later back at the festival grounds, percussionist and singer Mariá Portugal’s EROSÃO septet took the stage in the rapidly heating up early afternoon. The music began with a brass fanfare as the group walked-on the stage and transitioned to Portugal singing over polyrhythmic accompaniment. Concentrated on a repertoire of songs that drew heavily on her Brazilian background, Portugal’s vocals took center stage, while the high-powered group of saxophonists Lotte Anker and Angelika Niescier , trombonists Matthias Müller and Moritz Wesp , tubist Carl Ludwig Hübsch and bassist Reza Askari provided solid support. Afterwards in the Huettenwerk building, the duo of Mohammad Mostafa Heydarian and Valentin Portron , performing on the traditional Iranian tanbur and bendir - a stringed instrument and hand drum - continued the expansion of the festival’s musical purview. Impro-Concert: Tony Buck, Matthias Mueller, Taito Saito (workshop) Two improvisation sessions, tucked away in the workshop building, injected a bit of the unexpected into the afternoon. The first introduced the British woodwindist Tamar Osborn with the American bassist Nick Dunston and drummer Gerry Hemingway . This first meeting proved fruitful. Clicking quickly, Osborn leaned into the deeper registers of her baritone sax, while Hemingway contributed a lithe, but full, pulse and Dunston provided a melodically swinging bridge between the two. The later improvisation session joined three Berlin based improvisors who have been in each other’s orbits but never played together before. Vibraphonist Taiko Saito , trombonist Matthias Müller and drummer Tony Buck played a set ranging from contemplative to combustive. Aki Takase, Robert Landfermann, Christian Lillinger. (c) Cristina Marx/Photomusix The mid-afternoon offered both unforgiving sun and an excellent set from pianist Aki Takase who was performing her upbeat, complex, and often humor-laced music with drummer Christian Lillinger and bassist Robert Landfermann on the main stage. The trio’s music is impressive, Lillinger, with his agitated, driving approach is a perfect rhythmic partner for Takase’s own intensity, and Landfermann’s rhythmic and melodic playing adds a nicely fitting layer. Nearing the end of the set, a dramatic moment ensured when Takase suddenly collapsed from the heat. Fortunately, it was reported that the pianist was already on the move to the next concert in Austria that evening. Darius Jones & Otomo Yoshihide Quartet. (c) Cristina Marx/Photomusix A little later the shows were back in the biergarten, where the trees provided some relief from the 100 degree heat, and the Czech quartet Edemit added a jolt of avant-rock to the day while Neiscer and Portugal picked up in a duo form the earlier set. As the day began to cool, the action moved back on the main stage where Darius Jones and Otomo Yoshihide (alto saxophone and guitar, respectively) augmented by bassist Nick Dunston and drummers Gerald Cleaver and Yasuhiro Yoshigaki provided an electric set. Following a rousing Coltrane-like introduction, the rhythm section gave Jones a rumbling foundation for his soaring melody to which Yoshihide responded with a feedback-laden solo, pushing the music to an early peak. The music ebbed and flowed, from dark atmospheric wanderings to high-energy free-jazz explosions over pulsating rhythms. Afterwards, the UK-based Ill Considered featuring Tamar Osborn ( Idris Rahman on saxophone, Liran Donin on bass, Emre Ramazanoglu on drums and Osborn with various woodwinds) closed out the night with a set heavy on beats and Middle Eastern-tinged scales. The set ended with about half the remaining audience dancing in front of the stage. -- Perhaps in normal times, it would have been a disappointment but after the previous day’s oven-like disposition, the cool, rain-soaked grey morning greeting festival goers on Sunday was welcome. A church service in the Huettenwerk started the day for the faithful while out on the festival yard, the others were huddling under the drink stand tents sipping coffee while the bratwurst man started up his grill. First musical act, Richard Koch’s Ray of Light was the only one to be seen under the steadily raining sky. They began with the trumpeter playing a regal anthem and launching into a cheery, melodic tune filled with the folkish sounds of Fabiana Striffler ’s violin and Valentin Butt ’s accordion along with the rhythm support of Andreas Lang ’s bass and Nora Thiele ’s frame drums. The “gute laune” (good mood) music with its blend of up-tempo jazz, classical and folk elements provided a lighthearted start to another long day of music. Their timing was perfect too, as Ray of Light reached the end of their set, the first beams of sun reached the festival grounds. Have You Ever Been Experienced. (c) Cristina Marx/Photomusix The opening set was followed by Brandenburg Jazzpreis. Prize winner, guitarist Andreas Willers , who was to present his Hendrix inspired group Have You Ever Been Experienced , featuring a top-notch group of Berlin based musicians: Amy Green on vocals, Rieko Okuda on piano, Jan Roder on bass and Christian Marien on drums, was unfortunately too ill to attend. Despite this, the group, still gave a rousing performance, taking well-worn Hendrix themes and spinning them anew. Okuda took over the guitar solos with a distorted synthesizer, while Roder and Marien made sure the foundations were securely fortified. Most revelatory were Green’s vocals, which retained enough of the melody for song-recognition and enough improvisational liberty to free them from nostalgic interpretation -- for example, an updated interpretation of Allen Ginsberg’s Howl set to a free-jazz take of ‘If 6 was 9.’ The final two sets of the festival moved back into town to the church. The first was the Polish duo of vocalist Maniucha Bikont and bassist Ksawery Wójciński performing a set of haunting folksongs. Discovered through Bikont’s musicology research, the songs came from a disappearing tribe in the Ukraine, with themes that touched on the universal: suffering, responsibility and expecting better manners from the dead. Performed solely with voice and bass, the music filled the church mesmerizingly. Konradism. (c) Cristina Marx/Photomusix The closing set to the festival may have also been one of the most anticipated. Connecting the festival’s eras, trombonist and archetype of the original Peitz festival and East German free-jazz in general, trombonist Conny Bauer presented the large group Konradisms with an extended composition of “chamber big-band” that mixed generous improvisation and dramatic riffs. Joining Bauer was a cross section of a younger generation of German-based musicians: Nils Wogram on trombone, Maxine Troglauer also on bass trombone, Gerhard Gschlössl on tuba, Claudio Puntin on bass clarinet, Maria Reich on violin, Emily Wittbrodt on cello, Matthias Bauer on bass, Dag Magnus Narvesen on drums and Rieko Okuda on piano. Often breaking into small combos - trombone and piano, tuba and violin - the solos would grow intense and eventually congeal around common themes. A stand out was Puntin whose bass clarinet playing ranged from the sound of a flute to deep, woody resonance. After an intense two and half days of music, the two last concerts were a satisfying and full-circle-moment ending to the festival. Overall, one could sense a tilt towards the new - nights that ended with experimental but danceable music, a series of risky but successful workshop concerts with musicians meeting for the first time, an infusion of world-music elements, and a loosening, but not denying, deference to the past, showing a way forward. More about the Peitz festival: Review of the 50th Anniversary Peitz Festival Review of the Jazzwerkstatt Peitz Boxset Jazzwerkstatt Peitz website . Email This BlogThis! Share to X Share to Facebook

items._cn_summary: 这篇乐评记录了2026年德国佩茨Jazzwerkstatt音乐节的现场见闻与历史脉络。音乐节于1810年铁器与渔业博物馆阁楼举办，场地本身承载着浓厚的东德自由爵士记忆——1973年由Uli Blobel与Jimi Metag创立，曾汇集Petrowsky、Bauer、von Schlippenbach等两德及铁幕两侧的即兴音乐人，直至1982年被政府叫停，2011年由Blobel重启。2024年起其女儿Marie Blobel接手，将场地迁至鲤鱼池畔的渔业博物馆，并注入节庆氛围，包括儿童音乐循环站、电动小火车及啤酒帐篷等。评论提及周五首场演出由Hans Lüdemann钢琴与电子琴领衔的Trio Ivoire，呈现民俗与现代爵士融合的声响。整篇文章以文化史叙事为线索，融合了东德地下音乐史与当代节庆现场观察。

items.body: On his debut solo release, The Age Of Oddities, Dutch composer Rutger Hoedemaekers offers a cinematic record of glacial movement and emotive, ice-cool instrumentation. In some areas, The Age Of Oddities sounds like a traditional film score. Hoedemaekers has composed for film before, working closely with and alongside Jóhann Jóhannsson and Oscar-winner Hildur Guðnadóttir, and the influence of film composition seeps into the music, which is sleek, upright, and almost balletic. At the same time, Rutger pushes the boundaries through its electronic treatments, and The Age Of Oddities can be thought of as a progressive album. Processed and indistinct vocals are left to clutter an instrumental score, scrambling the stave, its electronic voices issuing forth a mangled form of morse code. This is the point at which The Age Of Oddities diverts from the traditional, as strings and brass intersect with soft electronic elements. The Budapest Art Orchestra’s 23-piece string ensemble, conducted by Viktor Orri Árnason, is the life-blood of the music, as are vocals (Kira Kira, Else Torp, and Laura Jansen), horn (Morris Kliphuis), trombone (Hilary Jeffery), and violin (Una Sveinbjarnardóttir and Viktor Orri Árnason). Rutger himself contributes trumpet, piano, keyboard, and electronics, and the resulting music is awe-inspiring, towering, majestic. Always composed and calm, the electronics fit perfectly with the more classical orchestration; one complements the other, instead of getting in the way. Amid soft and gentle interludes, one may find bombast and stormy undercurrents. All in all, The Age Of Oddities is a marvel, balancing the sensitive against the sharp, and the confusion of modern day life with the reassuring backbone of its strong melody. ww.130701.com

items.body: Break is Corey Fuller’s first solo record on 12k, and it fits the aesthetic of the label perfectly. The crashing of the waves – a metaphor for the struggles and troubles that inevitably come one’s way – is the theme of the record, but it’s also about finding peace and courage while in the eye of the storm, and treating that storm as a cocoon in which transformation is undergone. From the inky depths of a crushed soul to a clearing of the thunderstorm, Fuller notates something which for better or worse unites humanity in its entirety: struggle and heartbreak. We share in the same sorrows, and the same difficulties unite us. Humans are not too dissimilar at all – suffering is universal. We share more in common with one another than the news headlines will have you believe. Unity is stronger than division. As such, this album is an olive branch, a peace offering for the world. Aiming for a realization of the truth, Break reveals a nature common to everyone, awash in pre-installed morality. Fuller wants to elevate things, even while the two sides of peace and conflict continue to engage in warfare. Everything passes, so this thought can be a comforter when you’re in the thick of it, or in periods where patience is needed. It’s a virtue for a reason, and deep breathing can work wonders. Break’s quiet music unites in times of despair. Vocal exhalations mirror the crashing of waves against obdurate rocks, and Fuller’s sighing vocal, a passing cloud of vapour, translates the transience of life into sound. Similar to coming up for air during a trial, taking in a lungful of oxygen, the sighs offer respite. At sea level, high tide seems invincible, but when it recedes, scissor-shaped rocks reveal bones and old shipwrecks. Our lives are like that, too. On the surface, all appears well, but when you look underneath – when difficulties arise and hope recedes like the afternoon tide – you’ll begin to notice the threads of anxiety and fear. Worries and struggles affect the human body in a physical way, but Break’s inner peace can’t be shaken. Some of its heavier sounds attempt to drag the music down, but fragile and almost weightless piano melodies swim in the mix, keeping it afloat. A constant pull and release sweeps through the entire record, the air and the oxygen of the surface contrasting with life under the blue, bobbing line. Grainy distortion occasionally marks the tone, which fizzes like the surf. The background atmosphere remains light and clear to the point of transparency. When the music ascends and the background loses weight, the music floats in the air like a bubble, tethered only to its light, almost microscopic elements. Fuller’s attention to detail is second to none, and it all points to an intense period of considered work. The melodies are ushered out with care, and much of the music cycles around the piano, which was ‘recorded in a way that you can hear the bones, like an open ribcage, moving, contorting…’ ‘A Hymn For The Broken’ is a soft, stirring piece which would feel at home in a church. Its low-hanging, weighted progression contrasts with a lighter vocal, the two sides of the spectrum meeting, embracing. The sombre air distances itself from the promise of joy, cutting it in two even as it tries to find solace in a quiet, prayerful way. Sitting near the tail of the album, it’s a reminder, if one was needed, of the darkness before the dawn, and the tension before the break. Fuller leaves the reawakening until the last track, which gives the music a vulnerable air, all too aware of numbered days. While that might induce fear, it’s the natural order of life, and Breakaccepts that. Sometimes volatile, and at other times incredibly still, the album is described as an ‘emotional riptide, where violence and rest struggle to be the last voice’. The music stirs in the currents, seemingly broken by cruel theatre, while still dazzling with a gentle heart. There’s a bruised innocence about it. Although Break lies in the middle of a storm, it isn’t adrift. The struggles are its making, a defining moment, and it grows all the stronger because of the experience. When it can finally see an exit, anxieties fall away, dropping like a heavy backpack to the floor, making for the ultimate outbreath, and the ultimate release. Break by COREY FULLER www.12kmusic.bandcamp.com
items._cn_summary: Corey Fuller在12k厂牌发行的首张个人专辑《Break》以海浪冲击岩石为隐喻，探讨挣扎、破碎与内心平静之间的辩证关系。整张专辑围绕钢琴展开，钢琴的录制方式被形容为能听见骨骼在胸腔中移动与扭曲，脆弱的旋律漂浮于沉重的低频之上，形成持续的拉锯与释放。粒状失真偶尔出现，模拟海浪拍岸的泡沫声效。背景氛围轻透至近乎透明，音乐上升时如气泡悬浮于空中，仅由细微元素维系。呼吸声与叹息声被用作核心声学素材，将生命的无常转化为听觉体验。专辑在冲突与宁静之间寻找统一，既是个人疗愈，也是面向世界的和平提议，展现出极高的细节关注度与精雕细琢的制作理念。

items.body: Let me tell you straight up: the bucolic opening to James Osland and Finn Kelvin’s album “Colourless”, with its gentle droning tones, rolling waves, and wash of warm chords, is misleading. The ambiguous low rumble and jangling at the end of the piece suggests as much. The nocturnal hush of second track ‘Until Tomorrow Morning, Then’ quietly ushers in a darker mood by way of minor key glimmers, faint burbling electronics, and soft ringing; the groans from the deep and low throbbing of ‘Four Hands, Twenty Fingers’ only confirms the English duo’s chosen moody and introspective course. There’s not much information available online about our two guides through these quietly affecting sonic landscapes, but Discogs suggests they’ve collaborated before. The seven pieces on “Colourless” apparently emerged from live improvisations, and they share an openness of form in keeping with such origins. To my ears the sounds are predominantly electronic in nature, but there are plenty of ambiguous rumbles, crackles, and glimmers that could be derived from a wide variety of sources. A dog barks on ‘The World Isn’t That Easily Turned Upside Down’, and the buzzings, low glow, and swirls of hissing air mark this out as perhaps the most ambitious piece of the album, encapsulating the general sense of isolation without turning to outright pathos. The album ends with the quiet thrum of ‘Certainly It Was Hard To View This Mass Of People’, tones that may be from a guitar glistening like rays of sunrise reflected in dewdrops. It’s a return to the more bucolic mood with which the album began, and suggests perhaps an acceptance or coming to terms with the darkness in between. “Colourless” is a fairly short but intriguing glimpse into the sound world of Osland and Finn, leaving me curious to hear more from the duo. items._cn_summary: 这张专辑由两位英国音乐人合作，素材源自现场即兴录制，呈现出七段开放形态的声响篇章。开篇以田园牧歌式的温暖和弦与持续音调引入，但很快转入暗色调的内心独白：低沉的轰鸣、微弱的电子气泡声、模糊的嗡鸣与裂纹声交织，模糊了电子声与自然声源的边界。专辑中段最为野心勃勃的作品以狗吠、蜂鸣、气流漩涡等异质元素并置，在不诉诸悲情的前提下构建出一种孤离感。终曲则以类似吉他泛音的透亮音色回归开篇的宁静氛围，暗示对中途所经历的黑暗的一种接纳。整张专辑篇幅不长，但作为一次内省式的声景探索，展现了即兴创作中偶然性与氛围营造的张力。

items.excerpt:

items.body: Known for playing with County Joe McDonald, and for her experimental sound band The United States of America, Dorothy Moskowitz came back in 2023 with United States of Alchemy and their well-received release, Under an Endless Sky . In collaboration with avant-garde composer and filmmaker Francesco Paolo Paladino, and poet and music writer Luca Chino Ferrari, Songs of Compassion is eleven songs containing subversive and at times beautiful music, and richly evocative lyrics. Francesco Paolo Paladino and Luca Chino Ferrari | Photo by Maria Assunta Karini Songs of Compassion has two challenges for the listener. The first is the music, called variously avant-garde, ambient, modal, non-linear, and a few more. It is played mostly on pianos mixed in and out of the foreground, sometimes doubled, and sometimes out of phase, joined by strings, woodwinds, synth washes, and steely sounds. Initially disorienting, the music serves to remind us how locked our minds are to Western notions of harmonic movement. It speaks of alternative musical narratives much older and much further away. They are songs that subvert the song: more like Steve Reich than Steve Stills; more like Phillip Glass than Phil Collins. UNITED STATES OF ALCHEMY - Pale Wanderer At the same time, there are the poetic yet strikingly contemporary lyrics. �Pale Wanderer� talks about the fact that authoritarianism needs willing accomplices, describing what happens �When you make a deal with darkness.� UNITED STATES OF ALCHEMY (Dorothy Moskowitz, Francesco Paolo Paladino e Luka Chino Ferrari) by Silentes �Charlottesville� (written with the late Joe Byrd) evokes the time not long ago when torch-wielding nazis, proud of the metaphoric Ns on their tunics, chanted the antisemitic tropes paraphrased in Moskowitz�s words, �We�ll be one people, pure of race/No greedy throng could take our place� . Besides the overtly political lyrics, in the tradition of 1960s protest songs, there are also thoughtful meditations on mortality and our place in the universe. The message is high-minded yet sincere and direct. World weary and wise, Moskowitz�s voice inhabits the evocative philosophical lyrics with the authority of a skilled method actor. The melodies unfold like streams of consciousness, rising and falling, not following expected diatonic chord progressions, but honouring, instead, the value of each word. Moskowitz�s piano acts as another voice and sometimes a kind of Greek chorus commenting on the proceedings. The surrounding music frames, creates pulses and dissonances, and shimmers. The return of Dorothy Moskowitz with her renamed project has arrived in a moment quite similar to the times that spawned its predecessor. Political division, unrest, and uncertainty always generate artistic reaction, and United States of Alchemy roared back to life with their epic 24-minute opening track �Under an Endless Sky� in 2023, serving perhaps as an �In-A-Gadda-Da-Vida� for our times. Songs of Compassion continues to challenge how we think about our world. It�s music that defies the song form, while doing exactly what music is supposed to do�enrich the human condition. Find the artist online. items.label: Songs of Compassion
items._cn_summary: Dorothy Moskowitz 联合作曲家 Paladino 与诗人 Ferrari 合作专辑《Songs of Compassion》，收录十一首作品，以钢琴为核心，辅以弦乐、木管与合成器铺陈，构建出非线性的调式音乐景观。评论将其比作 Steve Reich 与 Philip Glass 的极简主义路径，强调旋律挣脱传统和声束缚，随意识流起伏。Moskowitz 的演唱苍老而智慧，承担哲思歌词的戏剧化表达。歌词兼具政治批判与对死亡、宇宙位置的沉思，延续六十年代抗议歌曲传统，同时呼应当下时代分裂。整体介于先锋古典、氛围音乐与吟唱传统之间，对熟悉实验语汇的听众具有持续吸引力。

items.body: A confession to begin: I�ve been a fan of Alison Cotton�s music for quite a while, so the announcement of a new album definitely brought me a frisson of delight. The Gods Laugh certainly doesn�t disappoint, with the same deliciously amorphous feel that�s defined her other work, drawing on folk, the avant-garde, as well as a sense of religiosity to make the music here, possibly best exemplified in �I Am!�, where she set a poem by John Clare, England�s great nature poet, to a transcendent melody over the constant underpinning of a lulling drone. While the playing revolves around her usual arsenal of viola, harmonium, hammered dulcimer, and piano, along with some percussion, on this album she also adds some drums, bass and synthesizer. The music is often improvised and captured in a single take, with an almost mystical, hushed sensibility that seems to reach through time, as with �I Still Know You are Calling My Name,� where the tune could have been plucked from an old folk song. Sprigs of Heather by Alison Cotton The centerpiece, however, is �Sprigs of Heather,� with an opening that recalls medieval sacred music that becomes a simple, slowly cascading, piano-led melody. It�s far from the longest track on the album, but a little pearl of perfection that carries the listener away. Sprigs of Heather by Alison Cotton The Gods Laugh is a memorial of sorts to Cotton�s father, who died in late 2024. There�s a sense of loss reaching across these tracks, most specifically present on �The Final Harvest,� a solemn piece about her father�s last visit to the allotment he loved so much. It�s suffused with tenderness that extends beyond words. Light and darkness bleed into each other across the music, and moods shift. It�s music that happily stands beyond category, with hints of so many things, but ultimately standing as Alison Cotton music, which might well be all the definition it needs. It will challenge you but also satisfy and move you. What more can you wish from music? Find the artist online. items._cn_summary: Alison Cotton 的新专辑《The Gods Laugh》延续了她一贯的跨界风格，将民谣、前卫元素与宗教仪式感融为一体。乐器编制以中提琴、管风琴、击弦古钢琴和钢琴为主，并新增了鼓、贝斯和合成器。多数曲目为一次性即兴录制，营造出穿越时空的低语般氛围。中提琴的运用贯穿始终，构建持续的低鸣铺底。《Sprigs of Heather》是专辑核心，开篇呼应中世纪圣咏，随后转为钢琴主导的缓慢级进旋律。整张专辑是对 Cotton 已故父亲的悼念之作，曲目中渗透着失去与温情的张力，光与暗在不同段落间交替流动。音乐难以归类，既有民间根源的暗示，又带有现代作曲与即兴的实验特质。

items.body: After the extra-terrestial explorations of Eventyrferd , the previous album from Norway's Camilla Hole Trio, in which sci-fi synth sounds were married with traditional material, their latest release Langs is rather more earthbound. But the quest to look beyond their own country's folk music continues. Camilla Hole's main instrument being the soprano sax, the influence of jazz is unsurprising and this is evident in the opening track �Springleik,� signifying a tune used to accompany the springleik dance from the west of Norway. Initially Hole takes the melody with Egil Kalman and Knut Kvifte Nesheim providing rhythmic support on double bass and drums respectively, with the overdubbing of Kalman's modular synth and Nesheim's vibraphone adding colour. But characteristically for this trio, in which assigned roles are never clearly defined or adhered to, things soon start to move around, with Kalman taking up the melody on his bass, playing the melody in unison with Hole, while Nesheim opens things out further rhythmically. As the whole piece takes on a much more improvisatory feel, Hole plays the melody one more time as things draw to a close. Langs by Camilla Hole Trio

items.body: Words by Justin TurfordThe Berlin-based Afro-fusion outfit Jembaa Groove have been on our radar since their debut album ‘Susuma’ brought their dreamy, light touch blend of soul and jazz-influenced highlife and Afrobeat to the world. Formed in late 2020 by Ghanaian percussionist, vocalist and songwriter Eric Owusu and Berlin born bassist, composer and producer Yannick Nolting (after a synchronous meeting whilst collecting their respective kids from kindergarten), Jembaa Groove was initially a 7-piece yet it has always been Eric and Yannick at the centre of the band and this new E.P. sees them working as a duo this time albeit with some very special guests in tow.Their musical backgrounds reveal much about where they are now. Eric was born in the Ghanaian capital, Accra but spent many years in Nigeria before developing into an accomplished sideman who regularly worked with highlife legends Ebo Taylor and Pat Thomas. Yannick’s peripatetic musical life has included jazz training in Germany before exploring traditional forms in various African countries, Brazil, India and Turkey as well as a number of years working with Lusophone artists in Lisbon. Add in a shared love of US soul and jazz and the richly coloured palette they work from is comparable to the UK Afrobeat-jazz septet Kokoroko, their laidback virtuosity similar but appreciably different. Yannick & Eric Their 2022 debut album ‘Susuma’ gained them immediate critical acclaim, smooth Afrobeat tracks like ‘Bassa Bassa’ showcasing their expert collage of Eric’s butter-rich multilingual vocals, jazzy chords, tight horn arrangements (check the Sir Duke-influenced horns on ‘Bassa Bassa’) and polyrhythmic groove sensibility. Not just anchored to Ebo Taylor style highlife, elements of Wassoulou music from Mali and Ghanaian (Akan people) Adowa became part of the band’s hybrid sound, a funky composite of influences that in their skilled hands feels remarkably natural. The second album ‘Ye Ankas / We Ourselves’ followed in 2024 and brought in guests K.O.G. and the great Gyedu-Blay Ambolley, the band stretching out in all directions but without losing what was now, an identity of their own.Onto 2026 and we have this four track E.P. ‘Be A Lover’, Yannick and Eric’s signature sound embellished by key guests from the UK, Nigeria and Mali. Having met the Nigerian highlife revivalist brothers The Cavemen at a festival in Amsterdam, Lagos came calling. In fact, Cavemen bassist Kingsley Okorie co-produced three of the tracks here and you can sense the pared-back space that The Cavemen have become synonymous with on these particular songs.The only song not involving the Nigerian brothers is the Yannick-produced opening number ‘No Pain No Gain’, which features East London-based but Nigerian-born, Ademola ‘Azekel’ Adesuyi. Viewed through an immigrant’s eyes, purposefully simple lyrics in English about resisting temptation and maintaining focus are sung beautifully over astral synths and glittering keys that Roy Ayers would surely love. Add sublime horns, a guitar motif by Nathan Badu that quietly embeds itself into your mind plus a rhythm section as relaxed and sensual as polyrhythmic percussion and bass can be and you have a perfectly judged Afrobeat-jazzy-R&B fusion deserving of a high chart position in a fair world. The brightly lit title track ‘Be A Lover’ sees The Cavemen’s Kingsley Okorie taking over bass duties as Lagos Afro-fusion artist Tim Lyre gives a heartfelt Afrobeats-esque vocal turn calling for love over violence - “be a lover, not a fighter”. The marriage of the classic 70s/80s percussion groove with polished guitar, synths and vocals (including harmonies from Eric and Kingsley) lends the song a delightful freshness, delivering quality Afro-pop without the omnipresent stain of autotune. The Cavemen: Benjamin James & Kingsley Okorie The Cavemen’s exuberant drummer and falsetto singer Benjamin James joins his brother Kingsley on the super-laidback ‘Obi’, probably the song most indebted to Ebo Taylor (or even the celebrated Igbo highlife legend Celestine Ukwu) on the record. Kingsley’s weary baritone intones softly over the most chilled of highlife grooves, his bass and his brother’s drums sitting back as dreamy electric guitars and languid horns take their sweet time. Benjamin’s wild falsetto interruptions bring a welcome friction to the otherwise elegant performance. The final song on this gorgeous record brings together a ‘supergroup’ of sorts. Jembaa’s Yannick and Eric and The Cavemen’s Benjamin and Kingsley are joined by one of the leading contemporary lights of Malian music, Fatoumata Diawara. Over (another) relaxed groove, the much-loved singer-songwriter and actress unveils her unmistakably powerful vocal in response to Eric’s quietly sung-spoken verses: a beautifully constructed contrast of human voices that is given another dimension from Benjamin as he throws out his own high-pitched exclamations.It’s great to see Jembaa Groove back and in such fine form. This E.P. feels like it just came together when the time was right, as unhurried as the tempo of the songs themselves. It’s also always a joy to discover new talents and I’ll be following Tim Lyre and Azekel from hereon. This is undoubtedly high quality Afro-fusion that can only build on their ever-growing global audience. 9/10.Released September 18th 2026.BUY HERE! https://jembaagroove.bandcamp.com/album/be-a-lover-ep

items.body: Sixteen tracks, most of them under three minutes, make up the first Scaled Alps album. The Los Angeles band released “Let the Alpine Play” on 20 July 2026 as a digital album on their own Blue Hell imprint, available on Bandcamp and on streaming services. Scaled Alps mix heavy rock, electronics and post-punk atmosphere under the low baritone voice of James Quentin Devine. Let the Alpine Play by Scaled Alps Devine sings, Anthony Percoco plays keys and guitars, Sean McCarthy plays drums and Steve Fishman plays upright and electric basses. Stewart Tuttle recorded the album at The Altar Studios in North Hollywood. The songs started as a set of self-recorded demos called “The Desertion Sessions”, cut in two sessions that ran through day and night and produced more than thirty tracks; sixteen of them were then re-recorded in the studio’s Big Room with Tuttle. On their Bandcamp page the band describe the result as “celestial, infernal crime spree music”. Devine described the project and the way the record was made in an email to Side-Line: “JQD is a low-voiced singer moving between heavy rock, electronics, post-punk atmosphere and stranger pop; the voice remains the stable identity while the machinery changes. The record itself was made rapidly and largely without a click, leaving breath, strain, drift and imperfections audible.” He points to “Southerly” and “Celestial Sighs” as starting points. ‘Let the Alpine Play’ tracklist The album runs “Another Clock Song (The 7th Unveiling)”, “Celestial Sighs”, “Southerly”, “Space/Time”, “Muffler (Chrome Viscera)”, “T.T.M.S. (Sunyata)”, “You Got H-O-R-S, You Want E Too?”, “Pink Diamonds”, “Neo Noir (Stelvio)”, “Selling It”, “Slow Motion”, “Impro (The Imp of the Perverse/The Pimp of the Inverse)”, “I Think We Met in Setagaya (Maybe it Was Seville)”, “Lemon Zest”, “Tentacoli” and “Throwaway Lines (Leo II)”. Only “Slow Motion” and “Lemon Zest” pass the three-minute mark; “Selling It” lasts 38 seconds. The band also publish an 18-page “Owner’s Manual” with the lyrics and the album’s visual material, and the full package of production WAVs and MP3s is offered as a free public download from the Blue Hell site. About Scaled Alps Scaled Alps is the band of Los Angeles singer and lyricist James Quentin Devine, who also records under his own name and as JQD, and of instrumentalist Anthony Percoco. The Scaled Alps name first appeared as a featured credit on Devine’s solo track “Cynical Ploy”, released on 5 May 2022, ahead of his solo releases “James Quentin Devine Plays the Saxophone For You” and “3-PIT” later that year. “Let the Alpine Play”, recorded at The Altar Studios in North Hollywood with Stewart Tuttle, Sean McCarthy and Steve Fishman, is the first full album under the Scaled Alps name and the first release on the band’s own Blue Hell imprint.
